flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time you felt overwhelmed or stressed at work with children present. What did you do to manage, not the kids, but yourself and your stress?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q4 Attempt 1]
Um, one thing that I learned that we're working with children when it comes to my emotions, the children could feed off of that. So I always try to like, whatever I'm going through when I'm feeling overwhelmed, even if it's work or just at home problems, I just keep it to myself. And I get through my day with a smile on my face, no matter what I'm going through. I make sure my energy is right, so it could be right for the children. So their energy is okay with me too. So getting through the day, once my day is over, then maybe I can handle my problems. But other than that, I try to get through my day. Once I clock in with a smile, I'm leaving out with a smile. Um, just keeping myself busy when it comes to the children, make sure the activities are fun for everyone, including myself, making sure that I'm just happy with them throughout the day, keeping my mind off things. I feel like the children, they really do like keep you moving and they keep you doing things. So your mind is very distracted and you're focused on them. So it doesn't really leave time for you to worry about like the problems that you have going on outside. Yeah. Outside of work. So your energy should be okay because they're distracting you from your problems.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or crying. Walk me through exactly what you would do and say, step by step
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q5 Attempt 1]
During that situation, I feel like I will first try to talk to the child if they are pulling away to see what is going on with them. If they can't communicate what's wrong, I feel like it's good to just give them that time to calm down. Usually, what I used to do was we had quiet places for a child to sit and just calm down and get their nerves right. And once they seem like they're calming down, we'll go talk to them and try to compromise for why they didn't want to do what they wanted to do. If they didn't want to get their diaper changed, if they didn't want to talk, if they didn't want to transition to outside or from outside to inside. And we'll just see what's going on. And then after trying to talk to them, if it leads somewhere, then we'll continue and we'll say like, oh, well, since you're okay now, do you want to try doing this? Or do you want to do that? Or if you want to stay outside, we can stay for five more minutes and then we're going to go inside. Or just. Try to like get the child to like trust you. You want to earn the child's trust. And I feel like that's very important when it comes to kids. You want to earn their trust. So talking to them and working with them, that would be my way of doing it.

flow_transcript_slices.question: How do you understand what a nonverbal child needs when they’re crying or upset? Can you walk me through how you respond in those moments?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q11 Attempt 1]
When a child is crying or upset, if they're nonverbal, from what I learned, like, working with children, sometimes children do use sign language, and if that child doesn't know sign language, I try to, like, communicate them in a way, like, showing them things, like, as in asking, like, if they're using, like, signs, like, if they're tired, I'll ask them, like, are you tired, do you want to lay down? Or if they're hungry, if they want to eat, if they want more of something, if they're upset and they're eating and they don't have any more and they're crying, I'll ask them if they want more using sign language, showing them different toys if they're crying and they were playing and someone took a toy from them, showing them toys, just trying to communicate with them in ways that they'll be able to respond if they're nonverbal.
